spatial_entity.notes: Late antique Sasanian polity, 224–651 CE. Historical geometry remains unresolved and must not be replaced by modern Iranian borders or a maximum-extent empire polygon.

claim.summary: Specialist legal-historical scholarship establishes slavery as a legally defined institution in Sasanian Iran. Enslaved people could be treated as property, inherited with estates, attached to agricultural land, and employed by Zoroastrian fire foundations. Sources of enslavement included captivity, descent, debt bondage and, under restricted conditions, sale of family members. This supports an institutional P3 classification without assuming that enslaved people formed a dominant share of the population or that practice was spatially uniform across the empire.

territorial_practice.notes: P3 is justified by explicit legal status, alienability/inheritance, agricultural and institutional slave labour, and multiple legally recognized pathways into slavery. It stops below P4 because the reviewed evidence establishes institutional structure more securely than empire-wide prevalence or demographic dominance.

source.title: BARDA and BARDA-DĀRI ii. In the Sasanian period
source.independence_notes: Dedicated specialist synthesis by a scholar of Sasanian law, drawing on the Mādayān ī Hazār Dādestān and Sasanian inscriptions.
source.reliability_limitations: The legal corpus is disproportionately informative about juridical categories and disputes and cannot by itself quantify the demographic prevalence of slavery throughout the empire.

source.reliability_limitations: Legal norms demonstrate institutional recognition and forms of exploitation but do not provide a census or warrant uniform territorial prevalence.

source.title: Zoroastrian Fire Foundations: A Portrait of Slaves and Slaveholders
source.independence_notes: Recent dedicated study in Slavery & Abolition focused on slaves and slaveholders in Zoroastrian fire foundations.
source.reliability_limitations: Institutional fire-foundation evidence is especially strong for one sector and should not be generalized mechanically to every locality or economic activity in the Sasanian realm.
